title: Teaching without preaching
hookLine: Epictetus points at sheep: they don't show the shepherd their grass, they grow wool
tomorrow: why did a king's sleepless night save Mordecai?

cards: Somebody takes up cold plunges, or a budgeting app, and now every dinner turns into a seminar on it. Even when they're right, you start dreading the subject.

Epictetus, a Stoic teacher, had a picture for this, and it's sheep. In his Handbook, he points at a flock in a field. Sheep, he says, don't bring up their grass to show the shepherd how much they've eaten.

teach.b: They digest it, and what shows is wool and milk. So, Epictetus says, don't show people your principles. Show them what your principles have grown.
Never call yourself a philosopher. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat; eat as one ought. When talk turns to big ideas among people who haven't asked, mostly keep quiet.
Then a story about Socrates. People would come to him and ask to be introduced to some philosophers, and Socrates would take them along to meet others. He didn't mind being overlooked.
That's the Stoic teaching: the proof is the life, and the life is quiet about itself. Matthew's Gospel has a line close to this, in its own words.

teach.h: BY THEIR FRUITS YE SHALL KNOW THEM.
teach.b: There, Jesus warns about false prophets and says: "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them." Fruit and wool: what a life produces is what tells. And an honest difference.
Matthew's Gospel ends with Jesus sending his followers out: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations." There, speaking is part of the call.

teach.h: ONE ASKS FOR QUIET, ONE SENDS OUT.
teach.b: Epictetus asks for quiet; the Gospel sends people out to speak.
Two different callings, and both trust that the words have to be backed by a life.

how: Stoic readers take Epictetus at his word: they practice where others can see, don't call themselves philosophers, and say little about principles unless asked.

o: giving sermons in a calm and friendly voice
passing on a way of life by living it, not lecturing
teaching only people who already agree with you

games.q: wool, not grass: tap the pairs.
p: show wool and milk, not grass
eat as one ought; don't lecture
took seekers to meet other philosophers

s: Epictetus's sheep mean you should hide your practice completely
the overcorrection. he says act on your principles in plain sight; just don't lecture about them.
in the Handbook, Socrates takes people who ask for philosophers to meet others
the Gospel and Epictetus agree on everything about speaking up
both say a life shows what's in it, but Matthew ends with Jesus sending his followers out to teach.

games.q: a new coworker asks why you never drink at team dinners. you have a whole philosophy about it. what fits Epictetus?
o: answer simply and briefly, then let how you live do the talking.
explain your full reasoning so she really understands the principle.
change the subject; it's private and really nobody's business.
games.why: at a dinner, Epictetus says, don't explain how one ought to eat; eat as one ought. say little, and let the wool show.

practice: Sit the way you would if someone could see you and you had nothing to explain: upright, easy, hands still in your lap. Let your face soften. For the rest of the sit, let the posture be the whole message.

wordCard.voice: Teaching without preaching: passing on a way of life by living it where others can see, and saying little about it unless they ask.

carryVoice: Carry this: show the wool, and let it do the talking, the way the flock does. Until tomorrow.
